title: Define an algorithm. Write any four characteristics of a good algorithm.
answer_html:
An algorithm is a step-by-step procedure or set of rules to be followed in calculations or other problem-solving operations. Characteristics:

  • Finiteness: Must terminate after a finite number of steps.
  • Definiteness: Each step must be precisely defined.
  • Input: Has zero or more inputs.
  • Output: Produces one or more outputs.
  • Effectiveness: Operations must be basic enough to be done exactly and in finite time.

title: What is pseudocode? Mention two advantages of representing an algorithm using pseudocode.
answer_html:
Pseudocode is an informal, high-level description of the operating principle of a computer program or algorithm. Advantages:

  • Easier for humans to read and understand compared to actual code.
  • Independent of any specific programming language, making it versatile.

title: Differentiate between time complexity and space complexity with one example.
answer_html:
Time Complexity: The amount of time an algorithm takes to run as a function of the length of the input. Space Complexity: The amount of memory an algorithm requires to run as a function of the length of the input.

Example: Mergesort has a time complexity of O(n log n) and space complexity of O(n), whereas Bubble sort has time complexity O(n^2) but space complexity O(1).

title: Define Big-O notation.
answer_html: Big-O notation is a mathematical notation that describes the limiting behavior of a function when the argument tends towards a particular value or infinity. In computer science, it is used to classify algorithms according to how their run time or space requirements grow as the input size grows. It describes the upper bound of the complexity.

title: What is the difference between best-case, worst-case, and average-case analysis?
answer_html:
• Best-case: The minimum time required for program execution for any input of size n.
  • Worst-case: The maximum time required for program execution for any input of size n. (Provides an upper bound).
  • Average-case: The expected time required for program execution over all possible inputs of size n.

title: What is asymptotic analysis? Why is it preferred over measuring execution time?
answer_html: Asymptotic analysis evaluates the performance of an algorithm in terms of input size (n) as it approaches infinity. It is preferred because execution time depends on hardware, compiler, and OS, whereas asymptotic analysis provides a machine-independent way to compare algorithms' efficiency.

title: What is amortized analysis? Explain the aggregate method in one or two sentences.
answer_html:
Amortized analysis calculates the average time taken per operation, over a sequence of operations, guaranteeing the average performance even if a single operation is expensive.

Aggregate method: It computes the total time T(n) for a sequence of n operations and sets the amortized cost per operation to T(n)/n.

title: Find the time complexity of the following code: sum = 0; a = 5; b = 10; sum = a + b; printf("%d", sum);
answer_html: The time complexity is O(1) (constant time) because there are no loops or recursion. The number of basic operations (assignments, addition, printing) is fixed and independent of any input size.

title: Find the time complexity of the following code: if (n > 100) x = x + 1; else x = x - 1; Also mention the best and worst case.
answer_html:
The time complexity is O(1). The condition evaluation takes O(1) time, and both the if block and else block contain basic arithmetic operations taking O(1) time.

Best case: O(1)
Worst case: O(1)

title: Find the time complexity: for(i = 1; i <= n; i++) { printf("%d", i); }
answer_html:
The loop variable i goes from 1 to n, incrementing by 1 each time. The loop runs exactly n times.

Number of iterations: n.

Final time complexity: O(n).

title: Find the time complexity: for(i = 1; i <= n; i = i + 2) { count++; }
answer_html:
The loop variable i starts at 1 and increases by 2 in each iteration (1, 3, 5, ..., n). The loop runs roughly n/2 times.

Execution count: n/2 times.

Final time complexity: O(n).

title: Find the time complexity: for(i = 1; i <= n; i++) { for(j = 1; j <= n; j++) { count++; } }
answer_html:
The outer loop runs n times. For each iteration of the outer loop, the inner loop runs n times. Total iterations = n * n = n2.

Final time complexity: O(n2).

title: Find the time complexity: for(i = 1; i <= n; i++) { for(j = 1; j <= i; j++) { count++; } }
answer_html:
The outer loop runs n times. The inner loop runs i times. The total number of executions is the sum of the first n integers:

Summation: 1 + 2 + 3 + ... + n = n(n+1)/2 = (n2 + n)/2.

Final time complexity: O(n2).

title: Find the time complexity: for(i = 1; i <= n; i = i * 2) { printf("%d", i); }
answer_html:
The loop variable i starts at 1 and multiplies by 2 each time. Sequence of i values: 1, 2, 4, 8, ..., 2k.

The loop terminates when 2k > n, which means k ≈ log2(n). The total iterations is roughly log2(n).

Final time complexity: O(log n).

title: Define algorithm correctness. Differentiate between partial correctness and total correctness with suitable examples.
answer_html:
Algorithm Correctness: An algorithm is correct if, for every valid input, it halts and produces the correct output as defined by its specifications.

  • Partial Correctness: If the algorithm halts, it produces the correct output (but it might not halt). Example: A while(true) loop that searches for an element and breaks when found. If the element isn't there, it might loop forever.
  • Total Correctness: The algorithm is guaranteed to halt, and when it halts, it produces the correct output. Example: A standard for-loop based linear search that scans an array from start to end and returns true/false.

title: What is a loop invariant? Explain the three steps—initialization, maintenance, and termination—used to prove the correctness of an algorithm.
answer_html:
A loop invariant is a condition or property that is true before and after each iteration of a loop. It is used to prove the correctness of loop structures.

  1. Initialization: The invariant must be true before the first iteration of the loop.
  2. Maintenance: If it is true before an iteration of the loop, it remains true before the next iteration.
  3. Termination: When the loop terminates, the invariant gives us a useful property that helps show the algorithm is correct.

title: Explain how loop invariants can be used to prove the correctness of a sorting algorithm.
answer_html:
In sorting algorithms like Insertion Sort, a loop invariant can be defined as: 'At the start of each iteration i, the subarray A[0...i-1] consists of the elements originally in A[0...i-1], but in sorted order.'

  • Initialization: For i=1, A[0] is just a single element, which is trivially sorted.
  • Maintenance: During iteration i, the algorithm inserts A[i] into its correct position in A[0...i-1], making A[0...i] sorted.
  • Termination: The loop ends when i = n. The invariant states that A[0...n-1] is sorted, which means the entire array is sorted, proving correctness.

title: Explain the difference between BUILD-MAX-HEAP and MAX-HEAPIFY.
answer_html:
MAX-HEAPIFY: Maintains the max-heap property for a given node, assuming its left and right subtrees are already max heaps. It has a time complexity of O(log n).

BUILD-MAX-HEAP: Constructs a max heap from an unordered array by calling MAX-HEAPIFY in a bottom-up manner on all non-leaf nodes. It has a time complexity of O(n).

title: Define a heap. Differentiate between a Max Heap and a Min Heap.
answer_html:
A Heap is a specialized tree-based data structure that satisfies the heap property, typically implemented as an almost complete binary tree.

  • Max Heap: The value of each node is greater than or equal to the values of its children. The largest element is at the root. Example: [100, 19, 36]
  • Min Heap: The value of each node is less than or equal to the values of its children. The smallest element is at the root. Example: [1, 2, 3]

title: Define the Divide and Conquer paradigm. Explain its three basic steps with a suitable example.
answer_html:
Divide and Conquer Paradigm

The Divide and Conquer paradigm is an algorithmic design strategy that solves a problem by recursively breaking it down into two or more sub-problems of the same or related type, until these become simple enough to be solved directly. The solutions to the sub-problems are then combined to give a solution to the original problem.

It consists of three basic steps:

  • Divide: Break the given problem into smaller sub-problems.
  • Conquer: Recursively solve these sub-problems. If the sub-problem size is small enough, solve it directly (base case).
  • Combine: Merge the solutions of the sub-problems to form the solution of the original problem.
Example: Merge Sort

In Merge Sort:

  • Divide: Divide the unsorted array of size n into two sub-arrays of size n/2.
  • Conquer: Recursively sort the two sub-arrays using Merge Sort.
  • Combine: Merge the two sorted sub-arrays into a single sorted array.

title: What are the divide, conquer, and combine steps in a Divide and Conquer algorithm?
answer_html:
The three main steps of the Divide and Conquer strategy are:

  • Divide: This step involves breaking the original problem into a set of smaller sub-problems. The sub-problems should represent a smaller instance of the same original problem.
  • Conquer: This step involves solving the sub-problems recursively. If the sub-problem is small enough (the base case), it is solved directly without further division.
  • Combine: This step involves taking the solutions to the sub-problems and merging them together to formulate the solution to the original problem.

title: Explain the general structure of a Divide and Conquer algorithm. How is it different from an iterative algorithm?
answer_html:
General Structure

The general structure of a Divide and Conquer algorithm can be represented recursively:

Algorithm DAndC(P)
{
    if Small(P) then
        return S(P); // Solve directly
    else
    {
        Divide P into smaller instances P1, P2, ..., Pk, k ≥ 1;
        Apply DAndC to each of these subproblems;
        return Combine(DAndC(P1), DAndC(P2), ..., DAndC(Pk));
    }
}
Difference from Iterative Algorithms
  • Control Flow: Divide and Conquer algorithms rely heavily on recursion (functions calling themselves), whereas iterative algorithms use loops (for, while) to repeat tasks.
  • State Management: In recursion, state is maintained implicitly by the call stack. In iteration, variables explicitly hold state (like loop counters).
  • Approach: Divide and conquer works top-down (breaking large to small), while dynamic programming or iterative methods can work bottom-up (solving small to build large).

title: Identify whether the following algorithms use the Divide and Conquer technique. Give reasons for your answer: Binary Search, Merge Sort, Quick Sort, Bubble Sort
answer_html:
• Binary Search: Yes. It divides the array into two halves, compares the target with the middle element, and recursively conquers only one of the halves. The combine step is trivial (returning the index).
  • Merge Sort: Yes. It divides the array into two halves, recursively sorts each half (conquer), and then merges the two sorted halves (combine).
  • Quick Sort: Yes. It chooses a pivot to divide the array into two partitions (smaller than pivot and greater than pivot), recursively sorts the partitions (conquer). Combine is trivial as sorting is done in place.
  • Bubble Sort: No. It is an iterative comparison-based algorithm that repeatedly swaps adjacent elements if they are in the wrong order. It does not divide the problem into smaller subproblems or use recursion.

title: Explain the advantages and limitations of the Divide and Conquer approach.
answer_html:
Advantages
  • Solving Complex Problems: Makes solving conceptually difficult problems easier by breaking them down into simpler, smaller sub-problems.
  • Parallelism: Sub-problems are independent and can often be executed in parallel on multi-core processors.
  • Memory Access Efficiency: Can be designed to optimize cache usage, as smaller sub-problems fit easily into the CPU cache.
  • Efficiency: Often yields algorithms with faster time complexities, e.g., reducing O(n²) to O(n log n) in sorting.
Limitations
  • Overhead: The recursion and function call stack overhead can make them slower for small inputs compared to simple iterative approaches.
  • Space Complexity: Deep recursion trees can lead to stack overflow or require excessive auxiliary space.
  • Repeated Subproblems: If not careful, overlapping subproblems can be solved multiple times, leading to inefficiencies (better handled by Dynamic Programming).

title: What is a recurrence relation? Explain its role in analyzing the time complexity of recursive algorithms.
answer_html:
A recurrence relation is an equation or inequality that describes a mathematical function in terms of its value on smaller inputs.

Role in Analyzing Time Complexity:

When an algorithm contains a recursive call, its running time can be described by a recurrence relation. For example, in Merge Sort, solving a problem of size n involves two subproblems of size n/2, and merging takes linear time O(n). This gives the recurrence:

T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)

By solving this recurrence relation (using methods like the Substitution Method, Recursion Tree Method, or Master Theorem), we can express the time complexity of the algorithm in Big-O notation (e.g., O(n log n)).

title: Solve the following recurrence using the substitution method: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n
answer_html:
Recurrence: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n

Guess: T(n) = O(n log n). We need to prove that T(n) ≤ c · n log n for some constant c > 0.

Proof by induction:

  • Assume the bound holds for n/2, i.e., T(n/2) ≤ c · (n/2) log(n/2).
  • Substitute this into the recurrence:
    T(n) ≤ 2 · [c · (n/2) log(n/2)] + n
    T(n) ≤ c · n log(n/2) + n
    T(n) ≤ c · n(log n - log 2) + n
    T(n) ≤ c · n log n - c · n + n
  • We want T(n) ≤ c · n log n. This holds true if:
    c · n log n - c · n + n ≤ c · n log n
    -c · n + n ≤ 0
    c ≥ 1

Since we can choose c ≥ 1, the guess is correct.

Result: T(n) = O(n log n)

title: Solve the following recurrence using the substitution method: T(n) = T(n/2) + 1
answer_html:
Recurrence: T(n) = T(n/2) + 1

Guess: T(n) = O(log n). We prove T(n) ≤ c · log n for some constant c.

Proof by induction:

  • Assume T(n/2) ≤ c · log(n/2)
  • Substitute into recurrence:
    T(n) ≤ c · log(n/2) + 1
    T(n) ≤ c · (log n - 1) + 1
    T(n) ≤ c · log n - c + 1
  • We want T(n) ≤ c · log n. This requires:
    - c + 1 ≤ 0 ⇒ c ≥ 1

Since we can find a constant c (c ≥ 1) such that the condition holds, the guess is correct.

Result: T(n) = O(log n)

title: Solve the following recurrence using the Master Method: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n
answer_html:

  • a = 2
  • b = 2
  • f(n) = n

Calculate nlogba:

Compare f(n) with nlogba:

f(n) = n, and nlogba = n. They are equal, which matches Case 2 of the Master Theorem (f(n) = Θ(nlogba)).

Formula for Case 2: T(n) = Θ(nlogba log n)

Result: T(n) = Θ(n log n)

title: Explain why Binary Search requires the input array to be sorted. What happens if Binary Search is applied to an unsorted array?
answer_html:
Why Sorting is Required: Binary search fundamentally relies on the ordering of elements. It compares the target value to the middle element and mathematically eliminates half of the remaining search space based on that comparison. If target < mid, it knows the target must be in the left half, because all elements in the left half are smaller than the middle element.

If Applied to an Unsorted Array: The logic breaks down. Comparing the target to the middle element gives no reliable information about where the target might be located in the rest of the array. The search might discard the half that actually contains the target, leading to a false negative (returning "not found" even when the element exists).

title: Explain how the Divide and Conquer technique can be used to find the maximum and minimum elements of an array.
answer_html:
The Divide and Conquer Max-Min algorithm finds both the maximum and minimum elements simultaneously by recursively breaking the array into halves.

  • Divide: Split the array into two halves.
  • Conquer: Recursively find the (max, min) pair for the left half and the (max, min) pair for the right half.
    • Base Cases:
      • If the subarray has 1 element, return it as both max and min.
      • If the subarray has 2 elements, compare them and return the larger as max and the smaller as min.
  • Combine: Compare the max of the left half with the max of the right half to get the overall max. Compare the min of the left half with the min of the right half to get the overall min.

title: Explain the best-case, average-case, and worst-case time complexity of Quick Sort.
answer_html:
Best Case: O(n log n)

Occurs when the pivot chosen at each step divides the array into two roughly equal halves. The recursion tree has a depth of log(n) and partitioning at each level takes O(n) time. Recurrence: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)

Average Case: O(n log n)

Occurs when the pivot randomly divides the array into proportional splits (e.g., 9-to-1 split or 3-to-1 split). Even an unbalanced split like 99-to-1 results in an O(n log n) running time, as the depth of the tree is bounded by a logarithmic function.

Worst Case: O(n²)

Occurs when the pivot is consistently the smallest or largest element, leading to completely unbalanced partitions (one sub-array of size n-1, and one of size 0). This creates a skewed recursion tree of depth n. Example: sorting an already sorted array when the first or last element is chosen as the pivot. Recurrence: T(n) = T(n-1) + O(n)

title: Compare conventional matrix multiplication and Strassen's Matrix Multiplication with respect to the number of multiplications and asymptotic time complexity.
answer_html:
FeatureConventional Matrix MultiplicationStrassen's Matrix Multiplication
Method Uses 3 nested loops to compute dot products of rows and columns. Uses Divide and Conquer, breaking n x n matrices into 4 (n/2 x n/2) sub-matrices.
Multiplications per step 8 multiplications for a 2x2 division step. 7 multiplications for a 2x2 division step (optimized mathematically).
Additions/Subtractions 4 additions. 18 additions/subtractions (increased overhead).
Recurrence Relation T(n) = 8T(n/2) + O(n²) T(n) = 7T(n/2) + O(n²)
Asymptotic Time Complexity O(n3) O(nlog27) ≈ O(n2.81)

Conclusion: Strassen's algorithm reduces the number of recursive multiplications from 8 to 7, bringing down the asymptotic time complexity. However, due to the overhead of extra additions, it is practically faster only for very large matrices.

title: Explain how the Divide and Conquer technique can be used for multiplication of large integers.
answer_html:
When integers are very large (e.g., hundreds of digits in cryptography), standard multiplication (O(n²)) is too slow. The Divide and Conquer technique (Karatsuba algorithm) speeds this up.

Process:

  1. Divide: Split each n-digit number into two halves (high and low parts).
    Example: X = A*10^(n/2) + B and Y = C*10^(n/2) + D
  2. Standard Divide and Conquer: Compute four partial products (AC, AD, BC, BD). This yields T(n) = 4T(n/2) + O(n) → O(n²).
  3. Karatsuba Optimization: Compute only three products recursively:
    • P1 = A * C
    • P2 = B * D
    • P3 = (A + B) * (C + D)
    The middle term (AD + BC) is derived as P3 - P1 - P2.
  4. Conquer and Combine: This reduces the recurrence to T(n) = 3T(n/2) + O(n), improving the time complexity to O(nlog23) ≈ O(n1.585).

title: Is merge sort a stable sorting algorithm? Explain.
answer_html:
Yes, Merge Sort is a stable sorting algorithm.

Explanation: A sorting algorithm is stable if it preserves the relative order of equal elements. In Merge Sort, stability is maintained during the merge step. When combining two sorted sub-arrays, if elements are equal, the element from the left sub-array (which appeared earlier in the original array) is explicitly chosen to be placed into the merged array first. By doing this, the original relative ordering of equal elements is preserved.

title: When would you select merge sort instead of quick sort?
answer_html:
Merge Sort is preferred over Quick Sort in the following scenarios:

  • Stability is Required: Merge Sort is inherently stable, whereas Quick Sort is not.
  • Worst-Case Guarantees: Merge Sort guarantees O(n log n) time complexity in all cases. Quick Sort can degrade to O(n²) in the worst case (e.g., already sorted arrays with bad pivot choice).
  • Sorting Linked Lists: Merge Sort performs excellently on linked lists because elements don't need contiguous memory access for random swaps (unlike Quick Sort). The O(n) auxiliary space requirement of Merge Sort is also reduced to O(1) for linked lists.
  • External Sorting: When the dataset is too large to fit in RAM and resides on disk, Merge Sort's predictable sequential access patterns make it the preferred choice.

title: Define dynamic programming.
answer_html:
Dynamic Programming (DP) is an algorithm design paradigm for solving optimization problems by decomposing them into simpler, overlapping subproblems. It solves each subproblem exactly once and caches the result in a table (memoization or tabulation) to prevent redundant computations.

Key Properties Required:

  • Optimal Substructure: An optimal solution to the overall problem incorporates optimal solutions to its subproblems.
  • Overlapping Subproblems: Recursive subproblems recur repeatedly rather than generating new instances.
simplified_html: Dynamic programming is like solving math problems on a scratchpad. When you calculate an intermediate answer once, you write it down so you never waste time recalculating it later.

title: Define backtracking.
answer_html:
Backtracking is a systematic algorithmic paradigm for solving constraint satisfaction problems by incrementally constructing candidate solutions within a state-space tree. It traverses candidate states using Depth-First Search (DFS) and applies bounding functions.

Pruning Principle: The moment a partial solution violates any problem constraint, the algorithm abandons (prunes) that entire search branch and immediately backtracks to the parent decision node to evaluate alternative choices.
simplified_html: Backtracking is like exploring an unfamiliar maze. You keep walking down paths until you hit a dead end, then immediately turn back to the last fork and try another path.

title: Explain N-Queens problem.
answer_html:
The $N$-Queens problem is a classic combinatorial constraint satisfaction problem that requires placing $N$ non-attacking chess queens on an $N \times N$ chessboard. Under standard chess rules, a queen attacks any piece along the same row, column, or diagonal.

Problem Formulation & Constraints:

  • Representation: A 1D array $X[1 \dots N]$ where $X[i] = j$ signifies that Queen $i$ occupies row $i$ and column $j$. This representation inherently satisfies the row constraint of exactly one queen per row.
  • Column Constraint: No two queens share a column: $X[i] \neq X[k]$ for all distinct $i, k$.
  • Diagonal Constraint: No two queens share a major or minor diagonal: $|X[i] - X[k]| \neq |i - k|$ for all $i \neq k$.

Solutions exist for all $N \ge 4$ (no solutions exist for $N=2$ and $N=3$, while $N=1$ is trivial).
simplified_html: Place $N$ chess queens on an $N \times N$ chessboard such that no two queens threaten each other horizontally, vertically, or diagonally. We record the board using an array where index is the row and value is the column.

title: Explain backtracking in the N-Queens problem.
answer_html:
Backtracking solves the $N$-Queens problem by positioning queens row by row from row $1$ to $N$. For each row $k$, candidate columns $col \in \{1 \dots N\}$ are systematically tested against previously placed queens using a bounding function Place(k, col).

Safety Bounding Condition: A candidate placement is valid if and only if no earlier queen $i < k$ shares the same column ($X[i] == col$) or the same diagonal ($|X[i] - col| == |k - i|$). If safe, the algorithm sets $X[k] = col$ and recursively explores row $k+1$. If every column in row $k$ causes a conflict, the current state is identified as a dead end; the algorithm abandons the subtree and backtracks to row $k-1$ to advance the previous queen to alternative remaining columns.

bool Place(int k, int col) {
    for (int i = 1; i < k; i++)
        if (X[i] == col || abs(X[i] - col) == abs(i - k))
            return false;
    return true;
}

By executing Depth-First Search with bounding, backtracking dynamically prunes fruitless paths, reducing the search space from $O(N^N)$ down to a small fraction of $O(N!)$. The search completes when all $N$ queens are safely placed.
simplified_html: Place queens row by row. Before setting a queen, check if earlier queens threaten that column or diagonal. If a row has no safe columns, backtrack to the previous row and try its next column.

title: Solve the 0/1 Knapsack problem for weights (2,3,4,5), profits (7,11,15,20) and capacity 5. Identify the  maximum profit.
answer_html:
Given 4 items with weights $w = (2, 3, 4, 5)$, profits $p = (7, 11, 15, 20)$, and knapsack capacity $W = 5$. We apply the 0/1 Knapsack dynamic programming recurrence:

$$V[i, w] = \max(V[i-1, w], V[i-1, w - w_i] + p_i) \quad (\text{for } w_i \le w)$$

Item ($w_i, p_i$)$w=0$$w=1$$w=2$$w=3$$w=4$$w=5$
$i=1$ (2, 7)007777
$i=2$ (3, 11)007111118
$i=3$ (4, 15)007111518
$i=4$ (5, 20)007111520

Traceback: At $V[4, 5] = 20 \neq V[3, 5] = 18$, Item 4 is selected. The remaining capacity becomes $5 - 5 = 0$. The optimal item set is $\{\text{Item 4}\}$ with total weight $5$ and Maximum Profit = 20.
simplified_html: We build a table comparing item combinations. Items 1 and 2 give weight $2+3=5$ with profit $7+11=18$. Item 4 alone has weight 5 with profit 20. The algorithm selects Item 4 for maximum profit 20.

title: Explain the backtracking approach to the 4-Queens problem and show one valid arrangement of queens.
answer_html:
The 4-Queens problem positions 4 queens on a $4 \times 4$ chessboard such that no two attack each other. Backtracking systematically explores placements row by row, pruning branches when column or diagonal conflicts occur.

Backtracking Execution Steps:

  1. Row 1: Place $Q_1$ at column 1. In Row 2, column 3 is safe. In Row 3, all columns $(1,2,3,4)$ are attacked. Backtrack!
  2. Row 1: Move $Q_1$ to column 2 ($X[1] = 2$).
  3. Row 2: Testing columns yields column 4 safe ($X[2] = 4$).
  4. Row 3: Column 1 is safe from both earlier queens ($X[3] = 1$).
  5. Row 4: Testing columns reveals column 3 is safe ($X[4] = 3$).

Valid Arrangement: The resulting solution vector is $X = [2, 4, 1, 3]$ (placing queens at $(1,2), (2,4), (3,1), (4,3)$), where all column and diagonal constraints are completely satisfied.
simplified_html: Place queens row by row. Starting Queen 1 at column 1 leads to an impasse on row 3. Backtracking moves Queen 1 to column 2, leading to the valid configuration: columns 2, 4, 1, and 3.

title: Define overlapping subproblems.
answer_html:
Overlapping subproblems is a fundamental property of problems where recursive decomposition solves the identical smaller subproblems repeatedly rather than creating unique ones.

Unlike Divide and Conquer (which divides problems into independent, disjoint subproblems like Merge Sort), Dynamic Programming caches the results of overlapping subproblems in memory tables (memoization or tabulation). This avoids exponential recalculation, reducing runtime to polynomial order (e.g., computing Fibonacci numbers or LCS).
simplified_html: A problem has overlapping subproblems when computing the final answer repeatedly requires solving the exact same smaller subproblems, like calculating $F(3)$ multiple times while finding $F(5)$.

title: Using denominations 3,2,1, find the coins selected by dynamic programming for amount 6.
answer_html:
For amount $A = 6$ and coin denominations $D = \{3, 2, 1\}$, the DP recurrence minimizes total coins:

$$dp[v] = 1 + \min_{c \in D, c \le v} dp[v - c], \quad dp[0] = 0$$

Table Progression: $dp[1]=1$, $dp[2]=1$, $dp[3]=1$, $dp[4]=2$, $dp[5]=2$, and $dp[6]=1+dp[3]=2$.

Selected Coins: Backtracking from amount 6 picks coin 3 (remaining 3), then picks another coin 3. Thus, the optimal selection is two coins: $\{3, 3\}$.
simplified_html: DP computes minimum coins for each value up to 6. At 6, taking a 3-coin leaves remainder 3, which needs one more 3-coin. Selected coins: two 3s, totaling 2 coins.

title: For activities with start times (2,4,1,5,7,8) and finish times (3,5,6,7,9,11) select a maximum compatible set using the greedy strategy.
answer_html:
The greedy strategy sorts activities by ascending finish times and chooses non-overlapping activities whose start time is $\ge$ previous finish time.

Given sorted intervals $A_1(2,3), A_2(4,5), A_3(1,6), A_4(5,7), A_5(7,9), A_6(8,11)$:

  1. Pick $A_1(2,3)$ (finish 3).
  2. Pick $A_2(4,5)$ ($4 \ge 3$, finish 5). Reject $A_3$ ($1 < 5$).
  3. Pick $A_4(5,7)$ ($5 \ge 5$, finish 7).
  4. Pick $A_5(7,9)$ ($7 \ge 7$, finish 9). Reject $A_6$ ($8 < 9$).

Selected Set: $\{A_1, A_2, A_4, A_5\}$ (4 activities).
simplified_html: Sort by earliest finish time and greedily choose non-overlapping tasks. We pick (2,3), then (4,5), then (5,7), then (7,9). Total maximum compatible activities selected = 4.

title: Find an LCS of X={ABCBDABDCBBDABC} and Y={BDC} Show the dynamic-programming approach and state the LCS length.
answer_html:
We find the LCS of $X = \text{"ABCBDABDCBBDABC"}$ and $Y = \text{"BDC"}$ using DP recurrence $c[i,j] = c[i-1,j-1] + 1$ on character matches.

Sequential Match: Character $Y[1]=\text{'B'}$ matches at $X[2]$, $Y[2]=\text{'D'}$ matches at $X[5]$, and $Y[3]=\text{'C'}$ matches at $X[9]$ ($2 < 5 < 9$).

Because all characters of $Y$ appear in sequential order inside $X$, string $Y$ forms a valid common subsequence. Thus, $\text{LCS} = \text{"BDC"}$ with LCS Length = 3.
simplified_html: All characters of $Y$ ("BDC") appear in sequential order inside $X$ at positions 2 ('B'), 5 ('D'), and 9 ('C'). Therefore, the full string "BDC" is the LCS with length 3.

title: What is a promising node in backtracking?
answer_html:
In backtracking algorithms, a node in the state-space tree is termed promising if it satisfies all problem constraints established so far and has the potential to lead to at least one valid, feasible solution.

Conversely, a node is non-promising if it violates any constraint. Backtracking evaluates nodes via bounding functions, immediately pruning non-promising subtrees and retreating to the parent node, thereby eliminating fruitless combinatorial searches.
simplified_html: A promising node is a partial solution that follows all rules so far and could lead to a valid answer. If it breaks any rule, it becomes non-promising and is pruned immediately.

title: Find an LCS of X=ABCBCABCAAB and Y=AC
answer_html:
To find an LCS of $X = \text{"ABCBCABCAAB"}$ (length 11) and $Y = \text{"AC"}$ (length 2), we use the Dynamic Programming table formulation $c[i,j]$.

Subsequence Analysis: Character $Y[1]=\text{'A'}$ occurs at index $X[1]$. Subsequent character $Y[2]=\text{'C'}$ occurs at index $X[3]$ ($1 < 3$). Both characters of $Y$ appear in forward sequential order inside $X$.

Since $|Y| = 2$ is the upper bound on common subsequence length, the entire string $Y$ is an optimal subsequence. Thus, $\text{LCS} = \text{"AC"}$ with Length = 2.
simplified_html: Characters 'A' and 'C' appear in that exact order in string $X$ at positions 1 and 3. Because $Y$ only has 2 letters, the longest possible common subsequence is "AC" with length 2.

title: Given Huffman frequencies 4,7,8,10 identify the first two combinations.
answer_html:
Huffman coding greedily merges the two lowest frequency nodes from a min-heap.

Given initial frequencies: $\{4, 7, 8, 10\}$.

  • First Combination: Extract smallest $4$ and $7$. Merge into internal node of weight $4 + 7 = \mathbf{11}$. Set: $\{8, 10, 11\}$.
  • Second Combination: Extract next smallest $8$ and $10$. Merge into internal node of weight $8 + 10 = \mathbf{18}$. Set: $\{11, 18\}$.
simplified_html: Huffman's greedy strategy repeatedly merges the two smallest numbers. First, 4 and 7 combine to produce 11. From the remaining set {8, 10, 11}, the two smallest are 8 and 10, combining to produce 18.

title: Compare greedy algorithms and dynamic programming with respect to strategy, subproblem handling and optimality.
answer_html:
CriterionGreedy AlgorithmDynamic Programming
StrategyMakes locally optimal choice at each step; never reconsiders.Explores all subproblem choices and combines their solutions.
Subproblem HandlingSolves subproblems top-down sequentially without overlapping storage.Solves overlapping subproblems bottom-up, memoizing table entries.
OptimalityDoes not guarantee global optimum for all problems (e.g., 0/1 knapsack).Always guarantees global optimum if optimal substructure holds.
simplified_html: Greedy makes the best immediate choice at each step without looking back. Dynamic programming systematically solves and remembers all subproblems in a table, guaranteeing a globally optimal answer.

title: Define a longest common subsequence.
answer_html:
A subsequence of a sequence $X$ is obtained by deleting zero or more elements without changing the order of remaining elements. A Longest Common Subsequence (LCS) of sequences $X$ and $Y$ is a common subsequence of maximum length.

Unlike substrings, elements need not be contiguous. The DP recurrence is:

$$c[i,j] = \begin{cases} c[i-1,j-1] + 1 & \text{if } x_i = y_j \\ \max(c[i-1,j], c[i,j-1]) & \text{if } x_i \neq y_j \end{cases}$$
simplified_html: An LCS is the longest sequence of characters that appears in the exact same relative order inside two strings, without necessarily being side-by-side (contiguous).

title: What is a state-space tree in the N-Queens problem?
answer_html:
A state-space tree in the $N$-Queens problem is an ordered tree representing all partial and candidate queen configurations explored during backtracking search.

  • Tree Structure: The root represents an empty chessboard. Level $k$ corresponds to placing the $k$-th queen in row $k$, branching across $N$ possible columns.
  • Pruning: Nodes violating column or diagonal safety are dead ends (non-promising) and are pruned immediately, while complete valid leaves at level $N$ constitute solutions.
simplified_html: A state-space tree is a branching diagram mapping out queen placements row by row. Whenever a queen threatens another, that entire branch is pruned as a dead end.

  1. Merge 1: Combine $m(2)$ and $p(4)$ into node $(6)$ with edge bits $0, 1$.

title: Explain how dynamic programming can solve the LCS problem. Illustrate the construction of the table using two short strings.
answer_html:
The Longest Common Subsequence (LCS) problem finds the maximum-length subsequence present in two sequences $X$ and $Y$. Dynamic Programming solves it by defining $L[i,j]$ as the LCS length of prefixes $X[1\dots i]$ and $Y[1\dots j]$ using the recurrence:

$$L[i,j] = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } i=0 \text{ or } j=0 \\ L[i-1,j-1] + 1 & \text{if } X[i] = Y[j] \\ \max(L[i-1,j], L[i,j-1]) & \text{if } X[i] \neq Y[j] \end{cases}$$

Illustration with $X = \text{"ABA"}$ and $Y = \text{"BA"}$:

  1. Initialize row $0$ and column $0$ to 0.
  2. For $X[1]=\text{'A'}$: $L[1,1]=0$, $L[1,2]=L[0,1]+1=1$.
  3. For $X[2]=\text{'B'}$: $L[2,1]=L[1,0]+1=1$, $L[2,2]=\max(L[1,2], L[2,1])=1$.
  4. For $X[3]=\text{'A'}$: $L[3,1]=\max(1,0)=1$, $L[3,2]=L[2,1]+1=2$.

Traceback: From cell $(3,2)$ with value 2, diagonal jumps identify characters $\text{'A'}$ at $(3,2)$ and $\text{'B'}$ at $(2,1)$, yielding the common subsequence $\text{LCS} = \text{"BA"}$ with length 2 in $O(m \cdot n)$ time.
simplified_html: DP creates a 2D grid matching string prefixes. When characters match, add 1 to the diagonal; otherwise take the maximum of top and left cells. Backtracking from the bottom-right corner reveals the LCS "BA" of length 2.
